title: How an AI assistant actually answers you
analogy: a very well-read autocomplete
stages: your text is cut into tokens
the model weighs everything in the chat
it predicts the next token, again and again
the reply streams out
catch: it sounds equally sure when it is wrong, so check what matters

title: The context window: why long chats forget
analogy: a desk with limited space
stages: everything in the chat sits on the desk
old pages fall off when the desk is full
key facts belong at the top
summarise and restart a long chat
catch: the assistant does not know what it can no longer see

title: RAG explained: giving an AI your own documents
analogy: an open book exam
stages: split your documents into pieces
search for the pieces that match the question
paste those pieces into the prompt
answer using only those pieces
catch: if the search finds the wrong pieces, the answer is wrong

title: AI agents versus chatbots
analogy: a clerk who answers versus an assistant who runs errands
stages: a goal replaces a question
the agent makes a plan
it uses tools to act
it checks the result and adjusts
catch: small mistakes compound, so keep a human check at key points

title: The role, context, task, format prompt
analogy: briefing a new colleague on their first day
stages: role: who the assistant should be
context: what it needs to know
task: the one thing to do
format: what the answer should look like
catch: a very long prompt can bury the task, so keep it tight

title: Why AI hallucinates and how to catch it
analogy: a confident improv actor who never says cut
stages: the model completes patterns, it does not look facts up
gaps in what it knows get filled with plausible text
ask for sources and reasoning
check one key detail somewhere trusted
catch: fluent writing is not evidence of truth

title: Prompting, RAG and fine-tuning: which one when
analogy: briefing a person, handing them a manual, or training them for months
stages: prompting: tell it what you want now
RAG: give it the right documents
fine-tuning: teach it a style or skill
start with the cheapest and move up
catch: most problems are solved before fine-tuning is needed

title: Automation: triggers, filters and actions
analogy: a doorbell that sets off a chain of events
stages: a trigger starts the flow
a filter decides if it should continue
an action does the work
test it with a real example
catch: automations fail quietly, so add an alert for failures

title: Temperature: why one prompt gives different answers
analogy: a creativity dial
stages: low temperature picks the safest next word
high temperature takes more risks
use low for facts and summaries
use high for ideas and names
catch: turning it up makes mistakes more likely, not answers better

title: Embeddings: how AI understands meaning
analogy: a library shelved by meaning instead of by title
stages: text becomes a point on a map
similar meanings sit close together
search by closeness, not by exact words
this powers smart search and recommendations
catch: closeness is not truth, it only means similar

title: Chain of thought: ask the AI to show its steps
analogy: showing your working in a maths exam
stages: ask it to think step by step
each step becomes context for the next
errors become visible
ask for the answer after the steps
catch: a neat chain can still be wrong, so read the steps

title: Break a big ask into small prompts
analogy: an assembly line instead of one worker doing everything
stages: split the job into stages
feed each output into the next prompt
check each stage before moving on
combine the pieces at the end
catch: one giant prompt hides which part went wrong

title: The Eisenhower matrix
analogy: sorting your mail into four trays
stages: urgent and important: do it now
important but not urgent: schedule it
urgent but not important: hand it off
neither: drop it
catch: if everything feels urgent, the sorting has not happened yet

title: Time blocking and where it breaks
analogy: booking meetings with yourself
stages: list the tasks that matter
give each a block on the calendar
protect the blocks like meetings
leave a spare block for surprises
catch: a plan with no slack collapses on the first interruption

title: The Pomodoro method
analogy: sprints with a built in finish line
stages: pick one task
work for one short sprint
take a short break
after four sprints take a longer one
catch: it suits tasks with a clear next step, not open ended thinking

title: Parkinson's law and deadlines
analogy: a suitcase that fills to whatever size it is
stages: work stretches to fit the time you give it
set a shorter deadline on purpose
define done before you start
review what you actually finished
catch: too tight a deadline lowers quality, so keep it realistic

title: Spaced repetition
analogy: watering a plant just before it dries out
stages: learn the idea once
review it just before you would forget
widen the gaps each time
test yourself instead of rereading
catch: reviewing too early wastes time and too late means starting again

title: Deep work versus shallow work
analogy: cooking a meal versus washing dishes
stages: shallow work is easy to interrupt
deep work needs a long clear block
schedule it at your sharpest time
batch the shallow work together
catch: deep work is a skill, so start with a short block

title: Capture, organise, review: a second brain
analogy: a kitchen with a prep station, shelves and a weekly clean
stages: capture everything in one inbox
sort it by what you will use it for
review the inbox weekly
turn notes into something you ship
catch: a perfect system you never open is worse than a simple one you do

title: Energy matching: put the right task in the right hour
analogy: using the best knife for the hardest cut
stages: notice when you think clearly
put hard work there
put routine work in low energy hours
protect the hard hour from meetings
catch: your best hours are personal, so observe before you plan

title: The STAR method for interview answers
analogy: telling the story of one project
stages: situation: set the scene briefly
task: what you were responsible for
action: what you did and why
result: what changed because of it
catch: most answers are all action and no result

title: T shaped skills
analogy: the letter T
stages: the vertical bar is one deep skill
the top bar is broad working knowledge
depth earns trust
breadth lets you work with others
catch: breadth without any depth reads as generic

title: Feedback that lands: situation, behaviour, impact
analogy: describing what a camera would have recorded
stages: situation: when and where
behaviour: what you saw, not what you assume
impact: what it caused
then ask for their view
catch: mixing in guesses about motives makes people defensive

title: Negotiation basics: interests and alternatives
analogy: two people building one deal, not splitting one pie
stages: know what you really need
learn what the other side needs
know your best alternative
propose options that serve both
catch: going in without an alternative weakens every move

title: Asking for help at work without sounding lost
analogy: handing someone a map with your route drawn on it
stages: say what you are trying to do
say what you already tried
ask one specific question
say thanks and report back
catch: vague questions get vague answers

title: A portfolio that proves your skill
analogy: a shop window instead of a catalogue
stages: choose a few projects, not all of them
show the problem and your role
show the result in plain words
make it easy to find and read
catch: quantity hides your best work

title: The five whys: finding the root cause
analogy: peeling an onion
stages: state the problem plainly
ask why and write the answer
ask why of that answer, again
stop when you reach something you can fix
catch: the first reason is usually a symptom, not the cause

title: Learning a skill fast: deconstruct, practise, feedback
analogy: learning a song by sections
stages: break the skill into small parts
practise the weakest part first
get feedback quickly
repeat in short sessions
catch: practising what you already do well feels good and teaches little

title: The cold message that gets a reply
analogy: making an easy yes
stages: show you read their work
say who you are in one line
ask one small specific question
make replying take under a minute
catch: asking for a big favour in the first message closes the door

title: A meeting that works: purpose, decision, owner
analogy: a flight with a destination and a pilot
stages: say the purpose in one line
name the decision needed
assign an owner for each action
send the notes the same day
catch: a meeting without a decision is a conversation, so use a message

title: Writing clearly: lead with the answer
analogy: a news story with the headline first
stages: start with the conclusion
give the two or three reasons
add detail only where it helps
end with what you need from the reader
catch: building up to the point makes busy readers stop reading

title: Reversible and irreversible decisions
analogy: two way doors and one way doors
stages: ask if you can undo the choice
for two way doors decide quickly
for one way doors slow down and gather facts
review the decision later
catch: treating every choice as one way freezes you

title: The habit loop: cue, routine, reward
analogy: a path worn into grass
stages: a cue starts the habit
the routine is the action
the reward makes you repeat it
attach the new habit to an existing cue
catch: changing the routine is easier than removing the cue
